executive_summary.narrative: The application exhibits potential vulnerabilities related to injection flaws, authentication mechanisms, authorization controls, and unsafe handling of dynamic inputs. Critical risks like W-001 through W-004 impact authentication and could lead to full compromise if exploited. Although unproven due to testing gaps, these are high-fidelity threats given their targeting of core endpoints. Priority actions should include sanitizing and validating all inputs used in login functions—particularly around the `email` parameter—and implementing robust access control over sensitive APIs such as `/api/Challenges/`. The test results have high confidence for proven cases and moderate-to-high confidence for untested but likely true positives.

findings.title: NoSQL Injection — in authentication logic (param `email`, POST /rest/user/login)
findings.status: tested, not proven (VERDICT: INCONCLUSIVE — The recorded request shows a valid login attempt, but without evidence of NoSQL injection or further exploitable behavior, additional targeted testing (e.g., with malformed email payloads) is needed to confirm or deny the vulnerability.)
findings.recommendation: Sanitize and validate the `email` parameter using a strict allowlist of safe characters before using it in any database query. Use prepared statements or equivalent technology-specific protections for NoSQL databases such as MongoDB’s query builders.

findings.title: Command Injection — via unexpected shell invocation (param `email`, POST /rest/user/login)
findings.status: tested, not proven (VERDICT: INCONCLUSIVE — Command injection via the 'email' parameter in POST /rest/user/login is plausible and maps to T1059 (Command and Scripting Interpreter), but requires live testing with payloads to confirm exploitability.)
findings.recommendation: Avoid invoking system shells with user-controlled input like `email`. If subprocess execution is required, use safe APIs like `subprocess.run()` with explicit command arguments instead of shell=True, and sanitize all inputs strictly.

findings.title: NoSQL Injection — name parameter may be embedded unsafely into a MongoDB-like query forming an exploitable injection sink (param `name`, GET /api/Challenges/)
findings.recommendation: Refactor MongoDB-like query construction logic to avoid embedding unsanitized `name` values in queries. Use object mapping libraries or frameworks that handle this securely out-of-the-box.

findings.title: Unicode Injection — name parameter may accept non-ASCII characters leading to inconsistent encoding handling across systems (param `name`, GET /api/Challenges/)
findings.recommendation: Standardize character set handling across front-end and back-end components. Validate and normalize non-ASCII characters where appropriate in the `name` field before processing.

findings.title: Authentication Bypass — via missing or spoofed session ID (`sid`) in POST request to `/socket.io/`
findings.recommendation: Implement server-side checks that ensure authenticated sessions associated with valid session IDs prior to establishing Socket.IO connections. Reject requests without verified credentials.

findings.title: Account Takeover — via email enumeration or weak login validation (param `email`, param `password`, POST /rest/user/login)
findings.recommendation: Prevent timing attacks from leaking account status by enforcing fixed-response times during failed logins. Apply rate-limiting and implement generic response messages regardless of whether emails exist.

findings.title: LDAP Injection — if LDAP-backed auth is used (param `email`, POST /rest/user/login)
findings.recommendation: If LDAP is used in authentication flow, validate the structure and content of the `email` value before including it in any filters, avoiding direct string concatenation into LDAP query templates.

findings.title: IDOR — name parameter may be used directly to query internal challenge objects without proper ownership checks (param `name`, GET /api/Challenges/)
findings.recommendation: Enforce access control policies at the `/api/Challenges/` resource level to verify ownership or visibility permissions before allowing retrieval based on user-provided `name`.

caveats: Produced by an autonomous pipeline with no human review. Findings should be validated by a security engineer before remediation is prioritised or the results are shared externally.
The crawl hit a configured limit after 4 pages, so the asset map is a lower bound and parts of the application were never seen.
API routes were extracted from client-side JavaScript. They are candidate routes the application references, not a verified inventory of its endpoints.
28 of 28 findings were not proven exploitable (W-001, W-002, W-003, W-004, W-005, W-006, W-007, W-008, …). They are hypotheses based on observed assets, not demonstrated vulnerabilities.
24 findings were never tested for exploitability (W-005, W-006, W-007, W-008, W-009, W-010, W-011, W-012). No claim is made about them either way.
Absence of a finding is not evidence of absence. This engagement covered what the crawler reached within its configured bounds.
